newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan shareholders grill scandal-tainted firms.
newsitem.headline: Japan shareholders grill scandal-tainted firms.

text.p: Irate Japanese investors grilled executives at two scandal-tainted blue-chip financial firms on Friday, but not everyone left satisfied with the replies.
More than 2,300 companies held annual shareholders meetings amidst public outrage over an epidemic of corporate scandals involving payoffs to racketeers and other management misdeeds.

But giant brokerage Nomura Securities and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, both embroiled in a high-profile racketeer payoff scandal that has led to more than a dozen arrests, took most of the heat from the floor.

"When are you going to stop just bowing and apologising?" asked a shareholder at Dai-Ichi Kangyo's annual meeting, where ranks of suited executives stood and bowed four times in expiation for top management's misdeeds.

Chief executives at the two top-notch financial firms apologised for the scandal -- the second to hit Nomura in six years -- and pledged to cut ties with racketeers and keep their hands clean in the future.

Japanese firms have long bunched their annual shareholders' meetings on a single day, a tradition which helps them to dodge questions about scandals and mismanagement both from legitimate shareholders and from professional corporate extortionists called "sokaiya" who target such events.
Executives also hold rehearsals for the events, which they traditionally hope to breeze through in 30 minutes.

Sokaiya try to extort money from firms by threatening to expose dubious business practices or stir up other trouble at shareholders' meetings. Some firms have also employed sokaiya to muzzle regular shareholders.
Racketeer scandals are nothing new, but the fresh affair has grabbed headlines just as Japan kicks off its "Big Bang" reforms to make its financial markets "free, fair and global".
Nomura's new president Junichi Ujiie, who assumed his post in May after a sweeping management shake-up, also pledged to cut off ties with sokaiya.
But some shareholders complained brokerage executives broke little fresh ground in explaining what really happened and why.
"The president answered questions deftly, but he dodged the real issues," said 33-year-old Ayako Yoshino, who left about half-way through Nomura's more than three-hour meeting.
Trading house Sumitomo Corp, whose huge losses incurred by a rogue copper trader stunned markets last year, was grilled by shareholder activists at its meeting in Osaka, western Japan.
Asked, however, when Sumitomo would make public results of its probe into the scandal, senior managing director Takashi Nomura simply said the firm would do so "at the right time".
Police were out in force to help companies cope and domestic media said 86 racketeers showed up at 16 meetings.
Not all the questions asked related to scandals or even corporate strategy.

"You're red in the face -- are you okay? Have you been drinking," a rough-sounding man asked Junichiro Miyazu, president of telecommunications giant NTT (Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp). Questions from that one investor ate up 30 minutes out of the meeting's total hour and 45 minutes.
"It cost me 500 yen (about $4) to travel to this meeting but there are no souvenir gifts. Why not?" another NTT shareholder asked.
Stung by charges of excessive secrecy, some firms have opened their meetings to the media or held them on other days to ensure accessibility.
Critics, however, say what's really needed is reform of management practices which shun proper disclosure.

"The culture is obsessed with quick and quiet shareholders' meetings and that sets the stage for a lot of other bad conduct including sokaiya payoffs and cover-ups of scandals," said Charles Stevens, partner in international law firm Freshfields. Corporate Japan, meanwhile, is seeking legal reforms that would reduce the items needing shareholders' approval, a change big business says is one key to reducing the sokaiya threat.
Businessmen also fault police for not providing real protection from sokaiya, who are often linked to crime syndicates and have murdered executives in the past.
"They can't really protect the executives and people get killed," said an official at business lobby Keidanren.
